name: Eight Off Solitaire
description: Eight Off is a sophisticated and highly winnable solitaire card game that served as a direct precursor to the ubiquitous FreeCell. Its defining feature is the namesake eight 'free cells' (reserves)â€”twice the number found in its more famous descendant. However, this extra mobility is balanced by a stricter building rule: cards in the tableau must be built down by the CORRECT SUIT, rather than alternating colors. This makes Eight Off a pure game of logic and strategy where almost every deal can be solved with perfect planning.

history.origins: Eight Off rose to prominence in the mid-20th century as part of the family of solitaire games that utilize 'cells' for temporary storage. It is often credited with inspiring Paul Alfille's creation of FreeCell in 1978.
timeline: Early 20th Century: Variations of 'reserves' games circulate in gambling and social circles.
1970s: Standardized as 'Eight Off' in computer solitaire collections.
Modern: Maintained as a standard challenge for solitaire enthusiasts who find FreeCell's alternating color rule too lenient.
history.cultural: Regarded as a 'Thinking Person's' solitaire due to its extremely high winnable percentage for skilled players.
history.evolution: The game shifted from simple foundations to its present form where sequence moves are heavily dependent on empty reserve calculation.

setup.players: One player only. Eight Off is a patience (solitaire) game played by a single person; there are no opponents or partners.
setup.deck: Single standard 52-card deck; all cards dealt face up into eight tableau columns and four reserve cells at the start.
setup.dealing: Deal face up: six cards to each of eight tableau columns, and the remaining four cards into the first four reserve (free) cells.
setup.equipment: Standard deck and a playing surface; no other equipment required.

rules.objective: Move all 52 cards to the four foundation piles, organized by suit from Ace up to King.
rules.gameplay:
1. Foundation Building: Move any available Ace to a foundation slot. Build up on it in the same suit (2, 3, 4...).
2. Tableau Building: You may move a card onto another card in the tableau if it is exactly one rank lower and of the SAME SUIT (e.g., 9 of Hearts onto 10 of Hearts).
3. Reserves: Any exposed card can be moved to an empty Free Cell. Only one card per cell.
4. Moving Sequences: You can move a correctly ordered suit-sequence if you have enough empty cells to 'shuttle' the cards. Movement is limited to (Empty Cells + 1).
keyRules: Only KINGS (or sequences starting with a King) can be moved into an empty tableau column.
Building is strictly SAME SUIT (unlike FreeCell which is alternating colors).
Cells can be used for any card rank.

strategy.basic: Prioritize clearing out the first four occupied cells as quickly as possible to increase your mobility. Never move a card into a cell if you can keep it in the tableau.
strategy.intermediate: Empty Columns: An empty column is more valuable than a free cell because it can hold a whole sequence of cards (starting with a King). Work toward emptying a column early.
strategy.advanced: The Suit-Lock: Since building is by same suit, if you have a high card of a suit (like a Jack) buried under a low card of the SAME suit (like a 4), that column is 'locked' until the 4 is moved. Identify and solve these suit-locks immediately.
tips: Always scan the tableau for Aces to move to foundations first.
Calculate sequence moves carefully; don't initiate a move if you won't have the cell space to complete it.
